ety.text: об- (ob-) + Его́р (Jegór) + -ить (-itʹ). It is likely connected to the feast day of St. George (Yegor, Yuri), on April 23 and November 26, when the terms of agricultural obligations would expire; the word thus means “to deceive someone by (or before) St. George’s Day”. Compare this proverb: вот тебе, бабушка, и Юрьев день (vot tebe, babuška, i Jurʹjev denʹ, “Well, Granny, there’s your St. George’s Day”), which is said about sudden misfortunes or dashed hopes.

ety.text: Inherited from Old East Slavic отъкрꙑти (otŭkryti), from Proto-Slavic *otъkryti, from *otъ- + *kryti (“to cover, hide”). By surface analysis, от- (ot-) + крыть (krytʹ). The sense "to discover" is a calque of French découvrir or German entdecken.
